articles.text: Millennium High School (MHS) graduated 18 seniors in the class of 2025 on Wednesday, June 4. Principal Irma Muñoz Daniels presided over her second class of graduates as the ceremony format modeled Millennium’s close knit family form. Every student walked to the podium and delivered thoughtful insights after staff introduced each at length, leaving no dry eyes in the Alan Harvey Theater. The ceremony allots for personal touches all through out, students spoke from their hearts through suppressed tears about overcoming challenges on and off campus, delving into personal lives in a way larger ceremonies cannot. English teacher Elise Marks provided background on three of her graduates, reading an impressive passage from soon to be UC Santa Cruz freshman Maile Imburg’s essay on Paradise Lost. “[Miley] takes on leadership roles not for power, but to genuinely solve problems,” Marks said. Millennium succeeds in providing a private school personal environment to students, in contrast to the pressure cooker that can be Piedmont High. Some Millennium students are heading to prestigious universities in the fall. Shakila Zuberi heads to UC Irvine, Ellie Willats will study at Lewis & Clark, Grace Rego is on her way to Chapman U., and Axé Johnson will be a freshman at Loyola University of Chicago. articles.text: The Piedmont High School (PHS) Class of 2025 bonded together one last time on Witter Field, Thursday, June 5, for the finishing act of their educational journey, Graduation Day. With broad support from parents, teachers, siblings and friends, the 205 students from the Class of 2025 received high school diplomas and entered summer as graduates. Those watching above kept temperatures not too hot, and not chilly, a perfect day by all accounts, inviting free wardrobe choices for all in attendance. Graduates, in purple caps and gowns, sat in chairs on Witter Field for the graduation ceremony. PHS Principal David Yoshihara showed a knack for the microphone and made a positive impression after his first year in the role. “Yo-sh” as his students call him, introduced student speakers Ellen Gudiksen, Salutatorian; August von Metzsch, Valedictorian; Ella Hughes, Senior Speaker; and Dean Olliphant, Senior Class President. “Life is about that resonance. Like a gong, it requires force to truly ring. To craft a legacy that rings, is to let yourself go,” said Hughes. Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Graduates share a laugh on Witter Field.

articles.text: The City of Piedmont is inviting the community to hear firsthand experiences of wildfire evacuations from community members, firefighters, and emergency managers at a community preparedness event this Saturday, June 14, at 10:00 a.m. at the Piedmont Fire Department. The event will follow the Fire Department’s citywide wildfire evacuation exercise and will also act as a debrief. At the event, community members will be invited to share their observations and questions from the morning’s evacuation exercise. Attendees will also have a chance to learn from speakers with real world experiences in recent wildfires, including an Eaton fire evacuee and Piedmont firefighters who provided mutual aid in Southern California. Piedmont Chief Dave Brannigan will discuss some of the City’s current initiatives related to wildfire mitigation and preparedness and how community members can get involved. Exercise instructions to be delivered via AC Alert Community members should look for an AC Alert notification around 9:00 a.m. on Saturday, June 14 with instructions for completing the exercise. Residents in the Blair/Scenic/Alta neighborhood will be asked to physically evacuate their homes. Elsewhere in the city, residents will receive instructions for an evacuation exercise they can complete at home. The at-home exercise is designed to be simple, easy to complete, and high impact. AC Alert is the mass notification system used by City and County agencies throughout Alameda County to rapidly disseminate emergency alerts to people who live, work in, or visit the County. AC Alert is capable of sending alerts by voice, text and email, posting to social media pages and sending FEMA Wireless Alerts. Those not yet signed up for AC Alert notifications can register at bit.ly/ACAlert. For more information, or to let the City know you plan to participate, visit piedmont.ca.gov/ EvacDrill.
articles.title: Speakers to share Firsthand Wildfire Experiences at Community Preparedness Event on Saturday, June 14

articles.text: Meet Jhene a shepherd mix at Oakland Animal Services. Jhene is a stunning, snuggle-seeking shepherd mix who walks nicely on leash and is very people focused. articles.text: Park Commission Chair Tom Smegal and Mayor Betsy Andersen jointly cut the ribbon. From left to right: Public Works Supervisor Nick Millosovich, Councilmember Lorrel Plimier, Park Commission Chair Tom Smegal, Mayor Betsy Andersen, and Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. The City of Piedmont held a ribbon-cutting ceremony last Wednesday, June 4, at 11 a.m. to celebrate the official opening of the new pedestrian bridge in Piedmont Park. “This is a very popular route in Piedmont Park. It’s at the end of Bushy Dell Creek, so it gets a lot of pedestrian traffic—and a lot of dogs get to come across it too, as it’s part of our off-leash area in the park,” said Parks and Project Manager Nancy Kent. The previous bridge, more than 30 years old, had fallen into disrepair. According to the city, holes in the wooden decking had been patched with plywood, and the original railings collapsed in 2023 due to wood rot. Public Works installed temporary side rails to keep the bridge usable until it could be replaced. The new bridge was designed Mayor Betsy Andersen (left), Park Commission Chair Tom Smegal, Councilmember Lorrell Plimier, Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales, Parks and Project Manager Nancy Kent, City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore, and Public Works Supervisor Nick Millosovich stand on the newly opened bridge. After the ribbon-cutting, councilmembers and City staff walk across the bridge.

The previous bridge, more than 30 years old, had fallen into disrepair. articles.text: Hello everyone! What a beautiful day to celebrate such an important milestone. How’s everyone doing? Before I go any further, I want to take a moment to recognize and thank the PUSD Board of Education, Superintendent Jennifer Hawn, Principal David Yoshihara, and the Parent Club selection committee for inviting me to speak today. I’m deeply grateful for the opportunity. And now, let’s give a huge round of applause to the parents and guardians, the teachers, coaches, counselors, band leaders, drama directors – everyone who supported and guided these graduates to this moment. Their dedication and love helped make today possible. I have three children of my own. Two of them have already walked across this field—one in 2021, the other just recently in 2024. So, to be perfectly honest, I thought the next (and likely final) time I’d be back at a Piedmont graduation would be in 2027, when my youngest is set to graduate… hopefully. Just kidding – she’s a great student. Most days. So yes, I’ve been here before – sitting up in the stands, squinting into the sun, thinking things like: “Wow, it’s hot,” “I hope the speaker is brief and brilliant,” and of course, feeling that overwhelming mix of pride, excitement, and a little nervousness about what lay ahead for my kids as they closed one chapter and prepared to open another. When Principal Yoshihara asked me to speak, I said yes— but with one request. I asked for the chance to sit down with some seniors and ask an important and not so simple of a question: What are your thoughts, feelings, goals, and concerns as you prepare to leave high school and begin the next phase of your life? I wanted to do this because no words I could offer would have meaning without first listening to you [students]. You are the heart of today. And the insights some of you shared with me were, in some cases, exactly what I expected. But in many others, they were surprising, thought-provoking, and deeply honest. While the views shared by the groups of students I spoke with may reflect the sentiments of many in the class, I also recognize that there are likely other perspectives that weren’t represented. Each graduate’s journey is unique, and I want to acknowledge and honor that diversity of experience. Among the predictable views shared were the excitement for newfound freedom, the anticipation of college life, the desire to explore new passions, and the bittersweet feeling of leaving behind the familiar comhow we live, work, and connect. These changes are not abstract— they are happening in real time, Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers was the 2025 Commencement Speaker at Piedmont High School graduation. forts of high school. The concerns echoed some of those feelings – the anxiety of the unknown, the pressure to succeed, the fear of making the wrong choices, and the sadness of parting ways with close friends. But what truly resonated with me were the unpredictable responses, the insights that spoke to the unique character of this graduating class. Some expressed a profound desire to make a tangible difference in the world, whether by helping others, contributing to their communities, or engaging in causes and careers they feel passionate about. Others spoke with a quiet determination to pursue unconventional paths, to forge their own definitions of success, and to prioritize personal well-being. One student shared a powerful metaphor: “High school was like walking a challenging but familiar path which has, to an extent, been paved for them. Now we’re at a point where the path must now be paved by us.” Others spoke eloquently about the importance of authenticity, exploration, and vulnerability and the courage to embrace failure as a necessary step towards growth. Several articulated a deep appreciation for the teachers and mentors who had guided them, not just academically, but as young adults finding their way. And others spoke about importance of community, specifically the importance of being part of one, with all of its good points and areas for improvement, nevertheless community was important. Graduates of Piedmont High School, your responses revealed a depth of self-awareness, a sense of purpose, and a refreshing blend of idealism and pragmatism. You are not just moving on; you are moving forward with intention. I want to take a moment to acknowledge the elephant in the room, something we talked about. Your next steps, whether they be to college, a gap year, the work force, the military, some mixture, or none of those, are happening at a time marked by extraordinary uncertainty and rapid transformation. articles.text: and they are shaping the world you are inhabiting. To add to that, many of you may soon find yourselves in places very different from the Bay Area. You may encounter perspectives, cultures, and values that challenge what you’ve known. That can feel disorienting. It’s natural to have doubts, to feel apprehensive about what lies ahead. But here’s what I want to say to you: Uncertainty is not just a challenge, it’s also an invitation. An invitation to be curious, to grow, to lead with empathy, and to adapt. And as you do, hold tightly to the values that define you. Let them be your compass, not your anchor, guiding you without limiting your ability to engage with others, particularly others with different views. Values rooted in integrity, compassion, equity, and respect—these are not to be sacrificed for the sake of fitting in or going along. They are the foundation on which you will build meaningful relationships and a purposeful life. You’ve been educated in one of the most dynamic and forward-thinking regions in the country. You are equipped with the tools to think critically, to ask bold questions, and to build bridges where others see divides. So as you enter this next chapter, don’t back away from the unknown. Face it with courage to explore, humility to learn, and a steady commitment to growing, without losing sight of the values that define you. The future is uncertain by nature, but that’s your call to step forward, stay grounded in your values, and meet it with the resilience it requires. Carry forward the lessons you’ve learned here, both in and outside the classroom. And don’t hesitate to lean on your support systems, your family, your friends, your teachers, as you navigate what comes next. Give yourself room to stumble. Be willing to take detours. Redefine success as you go because life is rarely a straight path, and it’s often in the unexpected twists and turns that you discover who you really are. And finally, lead with kindness. Let empathy and service guide your actions. The world needs your talents, your perspective, and your heart. Use what you’ve learned not just to succeed—but to uplift others and build stronger communities. Graduates, I stand before you today not just as the Chief of Police, but as a proud parent of Piedmont students, a neighbor, and someone who sees in each of you the strength, insight, and compassion that our future depends on. Class of 2025, you did it! Celebrate this milestone with pride, carry your values with confidence, and step boldly into the future you will help shape. The world is waiting, and I, for one, can’t wait to see what you’ll do with it. articles.text: Valedictorian Good afternoon everyone, and thank you, Ellen. As she said, I’m Gus, and I’m honored to be standing here in front of the class of 2025! On behalf of my whole class, I’d like to reiterate our gratitude to everyone who is here today—our entire Piedmont family—family, remember that—for the time and energy you have invested to get us to this point! Most of all, thank you to our parents. As much as your snarky 17 or 18-year-old might have told you they don’t care if you show up to their events— and I’m sure they have: I got a lot of texts before prom from kids who really wanted me to give them an out by telling them that their parents were not invited to my house to take photos of them; we truly do appreciate you all. Special shoutout to my mom, who has not only sacrificed so much for me but also for the entire Piedmont community. I know it’s an odd image now, but I remember when she would physically put me on her shoulders so I could see over a crowd. She was not the first person to put someone on her shoulders. Sir Issac Newton once said “If I have seen further than others, it is by standing on the shoulders of giants,” and our parents are the prime example of this. Literally and metaphorically, they’ve lifted us up throughout our childhoods. It’s not just them, either. I remember in fourth grade at Wildwood when we first got access to the computer lab and were doing the most basic of things, but to us, Scratch was like magic, imparted upon us by Ms. Cheung. Of course, a few of us, instead of paying attention, immediately installed Minecraft on our computers. When Durant stood on Aristotle’s shoulders, he added value by allowing us to derive meaning from unintelligible (to most of us) Ancient Greek. articles.text: Salutatorian, Class of 2025 Welcome everyone to the graduation of Piedmont High School’s class of 2025 at Witter Field, where we’re all glad to not be running the mile today. Instead, we’re here to celebrate, and I would like to extend the biggest thank you to everybody gathered. Teachers, faculty, family, friends, mentors, your support to all of us during the 18 some years of our lives has been invaluable in getting us to this finish line. I have a confession to make. I have been staring at the glowing green reminders widget on my to-do list, particularly the looming word graduation and feeling sick to my stomach. In fact, it was more on my to-do list than anything else. I’m sure all of us discovered the never-ending nature of a to-do list, constantly growing, lurking, demanding our attention. Though, it’s clear we’ve gotten very good at getting things done. It’s a relatively universal experience to have finally taken the Chem test hanging over your head for weeks just to be assigned an essay on All Quiet on the Western Front in the next period. And it becomes obvious quickly that just checking off items and watching them disappear from a list is an unfulfilling existence, although for one moment it’s pretty glorious. With an already overwhelming and unconquerable list of tasks and obligations, it becomes easy to shy away from doing more. In my quest to be a more ‘productive’ person, every year I hop on the New Year’s resolution trend. And while my bed might be made for the month of January, after a few weeks it’s all but forgotten. This year, though, I did something different. My New Year’s resolution was a mantra: “I will not avoid doing something out of fear of embarrassment.” As small as raising my hand in English, or say, giving a speech at graduation to hundreds of people… This 2025 resolution unlocked something in me beyond the to-do list, another realm of opportunities: the “YOLO list” and the “what is important to me” list. For the “YOLO” list, anyone over 50 can turn to a younger audience member to explain onto the “what is important to me” list. It is for tuning into our interests and aptitudes. These lists hold the items that make our lives meaningful and unique, which translates into how we give back to the world around us. Ellen Gudiksen, Salutatorian When it comes to giving back, I know Piedmont would look very different if Juliana DeYoung had not decided all of her Title IX work was important on top of varsity athletics. Or imagine if Oliver Greenebaum didn’t choose to use his enthusiasm to brighten every space, from school dance circles to every single classroom. Alma Ruberto is so deserving of the Gail Dryden award for community service, and the ways she has changed and inspired our community are innumerable. These contributions may have started in some way as a task to complete, but these people continued because they found a purpose not from simply completing the tasks set in front of them, but from following a spark within them. In truth, every single person in this class has developed a unique excellence guided by their own values. Our happiness relies more on not getting caught up in the stuff we need to do, so we can find joy in the things we get to do. And sometimes to-dos are actually things we need to do (unfortunate right?), and sometimes we have to get it done and it’s going to suck. But we can’t forget to live outside of those parameters, because life itself is NOT a to-do list. We make meaning of our lives by daring to challenge ourselves, following our passions, and using that to find our individual roles within our communities. And sometimes, life should just be enjoyable. Today is a collective finish line for the class of 2025, and it is absolutely cause to celebrate; be proud, and savor the feeling. Ohmygosh. I cannot believe we made it. I encourage every one of you to ask yourselves as we step forward into the future, what are you choosing to do for yourself? Okay graduation speech. CHECK. articles.text: With the rise of the internet and social media, building and investing time in community and in-person connection is more important now than ever before. Fostering moments of intergenerational learning and frequenting places apart from home and work are effective ways to support overall wellbeing. Intergenerational learning is the way in which all ages can come together and learn with and from one another. The concept goes beyond just a transfer of knowledge; it fosters social and emotional growth for all. Different generations spending time together in and outside of the classroom helps to cultivate skills, build self-esteem and encourage mutual respect and empathy. Engaging in learning opportunities with people outside your generation is something to which not all of us have access; this is where the significance of a “third place” applies. The concept of a third place was first referenced by sociologist Ray Oldenburg in his 1989 novel, The Great Good Place. It is a space, separate from home (first place) and work (second place) that we can go to unwind, connect, and socialize. Such spaces can be hubs for intergenerational learning, providing the connection we crave and setting us on a path of lifelong learning. A third place can be the local coffee shop where you are a regular customer, a bookstore around the corner that you like to sneak away to after work, or even a park Check out Chabot workshops where you can relax and decompress with others after a long day. It is any space that facilitates social interaction where your attendance is not required. We have many places like this available to us right in our own backyards. East Bay Regional Park District is made up of 73 parks throughout Alameda and Contra Costa counties to the east of San Francisco. They are committed to facilitating learning outside the classroom and they provide fun, informative, and healthy things to do year-round. Chabot Space & Science Center aims to inspire and educate learners of all ages about the Universe and Planet Earth. The museum itself is a base for intergenerational learning with its volunteers and staff eager and willing to pass on their knowledge to Photo courtesy of JPJ Pictures aspiring scientists, space enthusiasts, members, and visitors. Chabot hosts a variety of programs and events that help you to engage with the world around you and deepen your societal roots: Family nature workshops, paint and sips, hike and sips, First Fridays, and so much more. These spaces and relationships enrich our joint well-being, reinforce the importance of education, and remind us that learning does not stop with age—it strengthens with connection. Let us build and support local environments where curiosity is lifelong, generations learn together, and everyone has a place they belong. articles.text: First seminar “The World of a Play” launches July 28 Shotgun Players, a community-focused theater company based in Berkeley, recently announced the launch of a new, six-part seminar series entitled Miriam’s Place with engagements beginning July 28. The new program series is dedicated to an in-depth exploration and community discussion about local live theater, held at Shotgun Studios, the company’s rehearsal space in Berkeley. Seminars are led by Shotgun Players’ artistic directors, performers, artists and other key theater staff members and creatives. T he si x sem i na r s a re designed to give audience members an inside-look at how a production comes together while getting access to a design run, rehearsals, and a preview show. Coffee, tea and light refreshments will be served at every session, and visitors will gain exclusive access to a live production. Miriam’s Place gatherings are hosted in memory of Miriam Schiffman, “a life-long learner with an insatiable curiosity and passion for bringing people together” said Artistic Director Patrick Dooley. Dooley leads the seminar series, offering an immersive look into his process as Shotgun Players’ founder and director, leading up to the premiere of Christopher Chen’s newest play The Motion. “[Miriam’s Place is] a great opportunity for theatre-lovers to really get a deeper understanding and appreciation for the production process,” Dooley added. The series runs from July 28 to September 29. Sessions take place on Mondays from 10:30 a.m. to 12 p.m. Enroll for seminars at https://shotgunplayers.org/ show/miriam/ or by calling the box office at 510-841-6500 x 303.
articles.title: Shotgun Players launches seminar series Miriam’s Place this summer

articles.text: Photo by Laurie Gordon Entrance to Building One, Treasure Island, location of Treasure Island Museum, featuring “Pacific Unity” sculptures by Adaline Kent, Jacques Schnier and Helen Philips Treasure Island Museum, a nonprofit that preserves the island’s little-known Pacific-themed heritage, welcomes Bruce Marwick, president of the Sacramento Art Deco Society, this Saturday to lead a discussion on the island’s historic sculptures. Visitors will learn more about the Gladding McBean artists who created many of the public art pieces for the 1939 Golden Gate International Exposition. The exposition was held on Treasure Island, between San Francisco and Oakland, to celebrate the city’s two newly built bridges. Photo courtesy of Rebecca Schnier Jacques Schnier working on a large bar relief artwork for the Fair — unfortunately, the artwork no longer exists. Jacques Schnier’s artwork created for the World Fair Gladding McBean was the largest maker of architectural terra cotta in the western United States and remains one of California’s oldest operating companies and a pioneer in ceramics technology. The company’s artists created sculptures and bas-reliefs for buildings around the country during the 1920s and early 1930s. In the late 1930s, they were commissioned to create monumental sculptural works for the exposition on Treasure Island. While almost all traces of the World’s Fair have disappeared, the City of San Francisco has made efforts to preserve the island’s history—including the surviving sculptures—since the museum’s founding in 1975. The event will also explore the life, work and legacy of artist Carlo Taliabue, who immigrated from Milan in 1924 to work for Gladding McBean in Lincoln, California. Taliabue created monumental sculptures for the exposition while in residence. The event is free, but registration is encouraged. Visit https://www.treasureislandmuseum.org/single-post/treasure-island-sculptors-from-gladding-mcbean to register. The program begins at 10:30 a.m. this Saturday, June 14.

articles.text: Photo by Stefan Cohen The San Francisco Gay Men’s Chorus returns to the city’s Curran Theatre for its annual Pride engagement. The San Francisco Gay Men’s Chorus (SFGMC) and Grammy Award-nominated nonbinary songwriter Justin Tranter will perform at the city’s annual Pride concert on Saturday, June 21, at BroadwaySF’s Curran Theatre. Founded in 1978, the choral group remains one of the most iconic and influential LGBTQ arts organizations in the world. SFGMC was the first openly gay chorus globally and has played a pivotal role in the gay rights movement through both music and activism. The group sparked a nationwide choral movement after its first public performance at a vigil on the steps of San Francisco City Hall, following the assassinations of Supervisor Harvey Milk and Mayor George Moscone. “The first number the Chorus ever performed, way back in 1978, was Holly Near’s ‘Singing for Our Lives,’” SFGMC Artistic Director and Conductor Jacob Stensberg said in a statement. “While we’ve made tremendous strides in the fight for acceptance and equality, that progress hasn’t reached every part of our community equally.” Stensberg added that, in shaping this year’s concert, putting emphasis on trans and nonbinary visibility and acceptance was at the forefront. “I knew I wanted it to be an act of solidarity. A way to stand with them, to honor their stories, and to lift up their voices not just for our audience, but for the world to hear,” Stensberg said. “I’m thrilled to share this concert and to celebrate all facets of Pride, from love and authenticity to respect, and yes, to protest.” Chris Verdugo, chief executive officer of the San Francisco Gay Men’s Chorus, said the group is “absolutely thrilled to return to the iconic Curran Theatre to celebrate Pride in a way only SFGMC can.” “There’s something truly electric about sharing this historic space with our community, especially during Pride season, when our message of love, resilience, and unity resonates even more deeply,” Verdugo said. “This concert is more than a performance. It’s a call for justice and a powerful reminder that music can be both joyful and transformative.” SFGMC returns to the Curran Theatre for its annual Pride event, performing alongside Tranter, the former lead singer of New York City-based rock band Semi Precious Weapons. Tranter has written songs for pop icons including Britney Spears, Gwen Stefani and Kelly Clarkson, and has served on the board of GLAAD - an organization that promotes LGBTQ acceptance in the entertainment and news industries – since 2017. Tickets for both performances are available now at https://www. broadwaysf.com.
articles.title: SF Gay Men’s Chorus, Justin Tranter perform at annual city’s Pride Concert June 21

articles.text: San Francisco Opera premieres Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart’s Idomeneo this Saturday, June 14, as part of its 2025 Summer Season at the War Memorial Opera House. Set in Crete following the Trojan War, the opera begins with King Idomeneo making a desperate vow to the god Neptune: to sacrifice the first living being he sees if he survives a perilous storm at sea. When Idomeneo returns to shore, the first person he sees is his son, Idamante— sending him into a moral crisis. The opera follows the king’s struggle with this promise, featuring performances by American tenor Matthew Polenzani and Argentine mezzo-soprano Daniela Mack as Idomeneo and Idamante. Music Director Eun Sun Kim conducts Mozart’s early masterpiece, marking her second Mozart opera at the company following The Magic Flute. This season’s production includes new staging by Australian director Lindy Hume, making her San Francisco Opera debut. Her staging emphasizes the tension between people and their environment, with projections of craggy coastlines and raging seas that mirror Mozart’s dramatic score. The cast also includes bass-baritone Jongwon Han as the Voice of the Oracle, tenor Samuel White as the High Priest of Neptune, and Olivier Zerouali, Georgiana Adams and Mary Hoskins in supporting roles. Five performances of Idomeneo will be sung in Italian with English supertitles and are scheduled for June 14 (7:30 p.m.), 17 (7:30 p.m.), 20 (7:30 p.m.), 22 (2 p.m.) and 25 (7:30 p.m.). The June 20 performance will be livestreamed at 7:30 p.m. Tickets are available at the San Francisco Opera Box Office (301 Van Ness Ave., San Francisco), by calling (415) 864-3330 or online at sfopera.com. Box office hours are Monday, 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., and Tuesday through Friday, 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Matthew Polenzani in the title role of Mozart’s Idomeneo for the Metropolitan Opera

A way to stand with them, to honor their stories, and to lift up their voices not just for our audience, but for the world to hear,” Stensberg said. “I’m thrilled to share this concert and to celebrate all facets of Pride, from love and authenticity to respect, and yes, to protest.” Chris Verdugo, chief executive officer of the San Francisco Gay Men’s Chorus, said the group is “absolutely thrilled to return to the iconic Curran Theatre to celebrate Pride in a way only SFGMC can.” “There’s something truly electric about sharing this historic space with our community, especially during Pride season, when our message of love, resilience, and unity resonates even more deeply,” Verdugo said. “This concert is more than a performance. It’s a call for justice and a powerful reminder that music can be both joyful and transformative.” SFGMC returns to the Curran Theatre for its annual Pride event, performing alongside Tranter, the former lead singer of New York City-based rock band Semi Precious Weapons. articles.text: The Big Sleep is one of many films shot in the 1940s and into the 1959s which is referred to as Film Noir or American Pulp, a genre created in post-WWII Hollywood and recognized for its dark, even ominous contrasting black and white tones and images. The stylized narrative usually features cynical, antihero cops or P.I.s, flashy villains, guns and murder. Women are considered femme fatales, often called “angel” or “sister,” some hard-boiled and able to push back when engaging in a distinctive double entendre repartee. The Big Sleep, directed by Howard Hawks, is based on the book written by Raymond Chandler, and adapted for the screen by William Faulkner. The film opens with private investigator Philip Marlowe (Humphrey Bogart), looking a bit rumpled, narrow tie and the iconic fedora. He is called to the elegant manor of an aging, wealthy individual General Sherwood. Of course, a butler greets Marlowe and asks him to wait in an expansive foyer while he goes to announce his arrival to the General. A young woman, named Carmen (Martha Vickers), comes slowly down a wide staircase and pauses to give Marlowe a provocative hello. And so the story begins. Marlowe is soon taken into an adjoining glass hothouse where the General is waiting, confined to a wheelchair, formally dressed and legs covered with a blanket. While Philip begins to perspire, he listens to the backstory explaining why the General needs his services. He has two daughters, wild-child teenage Carmen, and the older sister, Vivian (Lauren Bacall). It’s Carmen who has signed a number of gambling debt IOUs, and the holder of the notes wants to be paid. Part of this dialogue is exposition, and the words blackmail and photographs are mentioned. Marlowe agrees to look into the matter. His rate is twenty-five dollars per day. Typical of film noir is its complex, even convoluted plot. The Big Sleep is no exception. Just when the mystery seems about to be resolved, another character appears, and a new thread is pulled creating a new mystery within a mystery. Lots of cigarettes are smoked, guns are pulled, some are shot. Marlowe gets worked over in an alley, then tied up, and is rescued by Vivian. Outside it’s dark, heavy rain falling, wispy fog swirling, and headlights appear, coming down a narrow road. There’s gunplay. A gangster-type is shot and falls slowly to the wet pavement. This is all classic noir, and you don’t have to know what you don’t know to enjoy the very clipped, suggestive, fast-paced dialogue revealing the obvious chemistry between Marlowe and Vivian. Don’t miss Marlowe and Vivian driving off down a country road, thus ending the noir tale. The Big Sleep. Directed by Howard Hawks. Starring Humphrey Bogart, Lauren Bacall, Martha Vickers. 1 hr., 54 min, Rated R. Made in 1946, Now streaming on Fandango/apple tv/ prime. articles.text: Daniel Craig and Léa Seydoux in Spectre The James Bond film, Spectre, is the 24th in ne of Hollywood’s longest-running franchises. The first was Dr. No, released in 1962, starring the debonair and iconic Sean Connery. It’s been more than 50 years since Bond took stage center and captured moviegoers’ imaginations and there have been, over the decades, multiple incarnations of 007, secret agent, licensed to kill. Daniel Craig was the most recent actor to don the Bond mantle (now retired) and though initially he seemed a risky choice (he followed the intensely classy, upper crust Pierce Brosnan), Craig proved to be perfect, in a blunt, well-toned, thuggish way. In fact, Craig’s Bond was a hammer and every encounter with the seriously bad guys proved to be a nail, no matter that he is wearing designer tuxes, white dinner jackets, or elegant bespoke suits (his wardrobe is part of his allure. Regarding the film Spectre, it’s a wonderful ride. But one that requires the audience to pay attention, for its plot is at times maddeningly convoluted with twists that require perhaps more exposition than is necessary in a Bond film. This fourth Craig film (Casino Royale, then Quantum of Solace followed by Skyfall) is as solid as the previous Bond films and includes a threading backstory that ultimately leads to Spectre, a worldwide crime organization headed by a Franz Oberhauser (Christoph Walz, doing what has become his signature psychopath). A much-anticipated trope in these films is the first twenty of so minutes, which are meant to captivate the audience, telegraphing that the games have begun. Spectre doesn’t disappoint. In a brief air battle, Porco’s plane is damaged and he finds his way to Milan for repairs. In Milan is a young girl, Flo (Kimberly Willia Paisley), who happens to be an airplane mechanic and engineer and Porco hires her to fix his plane. As it turns out, there is another girl, Madame Gina (Susan Egan), and despite Porco’s piggishness, crushes on him. Meanwhile a pilot named Donald Curtis (Gary Ewles), a rival of Porco’s, is crazy about Gina. And so a competitive triangle is formed. Much of the interaction takes place in the Hotel Adriano where all the local flyers hang out, good guys and bad. The hotel is also where Gina sings. It all sounds a bit strange and convoluted, even eccentric, but it isn’t. In fact, the plot is spare, straight-forward, comedic and ideal for young audiences. Kids will enjoy immensely the premise of Porco and will find the handdrawn animation – skies filled with airplanes, floating among billowing porcelain clouds – truly breathtaking and poetic. Miyazaki has demonstrated repeatedly in his work a love of flight: airplanes soaring through cobalt blue skies, symbols of freedom. As Flo says in one scene, “These old planes are works of art.” And its those flying machines that border on the mythic encompassing excitement and fantasy and good-hearted fun. Porco Rosso. articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group had a lovely morning last Wednesday for a special walk. Recent news reports said there have been a higher-than-normal number of eagle sightings in the Bay Area. Air quality improvements in the area and a year of plentiful rain that have filled the reservoirs where eagles seek food could be behind the increase. A pair of bald eagles have been nesting in a eucalyptus tree at the edge of Mountain View Cemetery near one of the cemetery’s reservoirs. Their eaglets had hatched, but since they typically don’t leave the nest, or “fledge,” for 10 to 14 weeks, the new family would still be in residence. Additionally, a pair of owls in Dracena Park were the subject of a recent naming contest by the city. The walkers went down Highland Avenue to and up Moraga Avenue. Bird watchers had been on the corner of Monte and Moraga Avenues, but State Fish & Wildfire guidelines instruct viewers to stay at least 330 feet from nests. While eagles can be curious about humans and even seem to recognize individuals who regularly observe them, they are not inherently “friendly” with people. Bald eagles are territorial, particularly during nesting season, and can be aggressive when they feel threatened, especially when defending their nests or young. Moraga Avenue traffic isn’t bothering them, but eagles are generally scared by loud noises, large, moving objects, and the presence of humans, so it is good to view them from a safe distance. The walkers stopped at Mesa, the street before Monte, for some information about eagles. Bald eagles weigh 10-14 pounds and have wing spans of 6.5 to 7 feet. Males are smaller than females. Eagles are not built for speed flying, but they can fly at about 30 mph and dive at over 100 mph. Their large, broad wings suit them for soaring and scanning, not chasing and maneuvering. Bald eagles typically live between 20 and 30 years in the wild. The oldest bald eagle on record lived to be 47 years old. Young bald eagles are dark in color but develop their characteristic white head and tail at about four to five years. Eagles only live in North America and are especially prevalent near coastal regions or large inland lakes and rivers with healthy fish populations. They mainly eat fresh fish, which they snatch out of the water with their sharp, curved talons. When eagles can’t find fish, they will eat ducks, small mammals, and decaying animal flesh, often considered roadkill. . Nests are built with large sticks and may be lined with moss, grass, plant stalks, lichens, seaweed, and sod. They are usually about 4 to 6 feet in diameter and 3 feet deep, although larger nests have been seen. Eagles primarily sleep on tree perches, not in their nests, either at them or nearby, especially during the breeding season to guard their young. Eagles have a specialized mechanism in their foot that allows them to lock it while they are sleeping. Bald eagles come out during the daytime. They often eat after sunrise but can hunt anytime in daylight. Eagles’ eyesight is incredible. They can see a rabbit running up to three miles away or a fish down in the water, but eagles don’t have good night vision. They need to find a branch and tuck in at night until the morning. This is different from another type of raptor, owls, who are nocturnal and have excellent night vision. Eagles’ hearing is similar to humans, okay, but not great. They also do not have a very well-developed sense of taste and smell. This benefits them because they are scavengers. Their breeding season lasts from January through July or August. Bald eagles mate for life. Both the male and female work together to construct a nest, usually high in a living tree. They typically return to the same nest each year, adding new material with every breeding season, so Piedmont’s eagles may be back next year. Males and females share incubation responsibilities, but the female typically spends more time on the nest. The process of eaglets leaving the nest can be gradual, with the young ones initially branching out to nearby areas before fully taking flight. Before leaving the nest, eaglets may start going to nearby branches but still remain in the area. They often remain nearby for several weeks or even months, learning to hunt and fly from their parents. The parent eagles continue to feed their young even after they leave the nest. While bald eagles once nested along the entire Pacific Coast, from the Aleutians to Baja California, there were only 487 nesting pairs remaining in the lower United States in 1963. The decline was a result of habitat destruction and degradation, the use of DDT, and illegal shooting. In 1976, the eagle was officially listed as an endangered species, and conservationists took steps to save them. Bald eagles are protected under the Bald and Golden Eagle Protection Act which prohibits hunting, selling, possessing eagles, or taking their feathers, nests, and eggs. A 1972 nationwide DDT ban and restrictions on lead birdshot and lead fishing weights also helped restore eagle populations. By 1995, bald eagles were relisted as threatened. Seeing a bald eagle now is no longer considered rare. Populations have significantly recovered and they are now common in many regions of North America. Alaska has the most bald eagles in the United States, with an estimated population of around 30,000 birds, and about five now in Piedmont. articles.text: The First Mondays Reading Group met on June 2nd at the Community Hall with 16 readers on the patio outside the hall. Participating were Richard Siegel, Orrel Lanter, Peggy Shultz, Marion Lim Yankovitz, Bob Hall, Phyllis Van Kranenburgh, Phil Witte, Martin Levy, Hilary Honore, Bill Ahern, Mike Henn, Lisa Euphrat, Melba Yee, Carol Long, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased that Linda Sigel was with them for the first time. Discussion leader Priscilla Wanerus was away, so Phil Witte filled in for her. The readers were there to talk about How We Got to Now: Six Innovations That Made the Modern World by Steven Johnson, which was published in 2014, and in which he explores the history of innovation over centuries. The book presents stories of accidental wonders and beneficial mistakes. Specifically, the author examines the unexpected connections within six technologies: Glass, Cold, Sound, Clean, Time, and Light. He traces aspects of the development of modern life from discoveries in these areas to their often unintended and surprising consequences. For example, Johnson presents glass as the material that he feels has most changed human existence. He traces the consequences of its discovery to the invention of printing, the adoption of reading glasses, and the creation of the microscope and telescope. These advancements led to understanding the patterns of the stars and observing microorganisms. One reader also noted we probably wouldn’t have pet goldfish if there weren’t glass bowls. The invention of air-conditioning enabled history’s largest human migration to cities like Dubai and Phoenix, which would have otherwise been uninhabitable. Johnson stressed that many innovations were not the result of a sudden moment, but rather they were usually a long process involving a network of inventors and entrepreneurs. articles.text: Anything can be famous. If you don’t think so, picture the most famous subway grate in New York City – actually the most famous subway grate in the world. How can a subway grate become famous? By being the one that sends up busy gusts of air just as Marilyn Monroe stands over it in the movie, The Seven Year Itch. Monroe’s provocatively blowing skirt became emblematic of the film, and of her, but if your visual memory fails you, you can refresh it at Piedmont’s monthly Flix Fest next week, because The Seven Year Itch is on the bill. Participating were Richard Siegel, Orrel Lanter, Peggy Shultz, Marion Lim Yankovitz, Bob Hall, Phyllis Van Kranenburgh, Phil Witte, Martin Levy, Hilary Honore, Bill Ahern, Mike Henn, Lisa Euphrat, Melba Yee, Carol Long, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased that Linda Sigel was with them for the first time. Discussion leader Priscilla Wanerus was away, so Phil Witte filled in for her. The readers were there to talk about How We Got to Now: Six Innovations That Made the Modern World by Steven Johnson, which was published in 2014, and in which he explores the history of innovation over centuries. The book presents stories of accidental wonders and beneficial mistakes. Specifically, the author examines the unexpected connections within six technologies: Glass, Cold, Sound, Clean, Time, and Light. He traces aspects of the development of modern life from discoveries in these areas to their often unintended and surprising consequences. For example, Johnson presents glass as the material that he feels has most changed human existence. He traces the consequences of its discovery to the invention of printing, the adoption of reading glasses, and the creation of the microscope and telescope. These advancements led to understanding the patterns of the stars and observing microorganisms. One reader also noted we probably wouldn’t have pet goldfish if there weren’t glass bowls. The invention of air-conditioning enabled history’s largest human migration to cities like Dubai and Phoenix, which would have otherwise been uninhabitable. Johnson stressed that many innovations were not the result of a sudden moment, but rather they were usually a long process involving a network of inventors and entrepreneurs. Radio was an important exception: it was developed in one place at one time. Almost all the readers enjoyed it. The topics that Johnson covers are certainly ones that have changed how our civilization has advanced and how we live today. We tend to take much for granted, but it was fun to have a fuller understanding of what got us here. There was a lot of trivia in the book, but readers found it enlightening to see how one invention led to another and then to another. It made the readers aware of how fickle the flow of history and life can be with both good and bad consequences. There were some reservations about the book. The writing style seemed derived from television, and in fact the book has been developed into a PBS broadcast series. articles.text: Compiled Reporting on the Shortcomings of Tesla’s Electric Pickup Since its release in late 2023, Tesla’s electric pickup truck has been making headlines — not always for the right reasons. The Cybertruck’s weight, power and speed make it a formidable presence on American roads, but its futuristic design and unconventional features have raised serious questions about safety and practicality. In just 18 months on the market, the Cybertruck has already been recalled eight times. The most recent recall, in March, involved more than 46,000 vehicles after reports that an exterior trim panel could detach and create hazardous driving conditions. The safety concerns don’t stop there. According to a February report by Mother Jones, analysis suggests the Cybertruck has a higher fatality rate than even the infamous Ford Pinto. As of February, the Cybertruck’s fatality rate stood at 14.5 per 100,000 units — 17 times that of the Pinto. Rough around the Edges The Cybertruck remains a technological accomplishment among electric vehicles. It accelerates from zero to 60 mph in just 2.6 seconds and weighs nearly 7,000 pounds, with its distinctive stainless steel paneling and armored glass adding to its futuristic image. While the vehicle boasts a 5-star safety rating from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), concerns about pedestrian safety have followed it since launch. The sharp, rigid body panels that give the Cybertruck its signature look fail to meet European pedestrian protection standards, effectively banning it from European roads. Auto reviewers at Throttle House even tested the vehicle’s edges using carrots to simulate human fingers — and showed how easily the sharp steel peeled the carrot and how quickly the automatic trunk could snap one in half. “Borderline dangerous. I don’t care how much it costs, you’ve got to round these edges The memorial site of last November’s tragic auto-accident involving a Cybertruck. An image taken from crash tests on the Tesla Cybertruck by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA). out,” said reviewer Thomas Holland. Visibility is another issue. Holland called the Cybertruck’s blind spots “God-awful,” noting large gaps between the windshield and side windows, along with a rearview mirror blocked when the truck bed is covered. The rear camera provides some help, but not always reliably. Safety by Software — and Its Limitations Like much of Tesla’s product line, the Cybertruck relies heavily on its computer system to operate even basic functions — including opening the doors. If the system fails or loses power, doors may remain locked, forcing passengers to locate a hidden emergency release that Jalopnik called “a dangerous nightmare.” That release is buried under a plastic panel and rubber mat at the bottom of the rear door. While instructions are available in the owner’s manual, most passengers wouldn’t know where to look — especially in a crisis, where seconds can matter. A Local Tragedy In Piedmont, these safety concerns took a tragic turn. Early on the morning of Nov. 27, 2024, a single-car Cybertruck crash took the lives of three recent graduates of Piedmont High School. The wrecked vehicle was soon engulfed in flames, leaving the community in mourning. As reported by Chase Hunter for the East Bay Times, witness testimony and the California Highway Patrol (CHP) report revealed harrowing rescue attempts. The Cybertruck’s doors could not be opened after the crash. Initial attempts to break a window with fists failed. A tree branch — about 4 to 5 feet long — was then used to strike the passenger-side window 10 to 15 times before it cracked. The window was pulled from its frame, and one passenger was rescued. Another passenger in the back seat tried to escape through the same opening but was unable to make it past the growing fire. The CHP investigation into the crash remains ongoing. Consumer Frustrations Mount Beyond safety concerns, Cybertruck owners have shared frustrations online. Videos of Cybertruck malfunctions have gone viral, and an entire Reddit community — “Cyberstuck” — documents breakdowns and glitches. In one widely shared story, a Cybertruck entered “limp mode” due to a front trunk alignment issue and had to be towed from a child’s baseball game. Tesla’s top-of-the-line Cyberbeast model sells for $100,000. Yet sluggish sales reflect the growing skepticism. As of June 9, International Business Times reported that Tesla was offering interest-free loans — essentially a $10,000 discount — to move inventory. Meanwhile, more than 100 unsold Cybertrucks reportedly sit in storage at a disused shopping center in Farmington Hills, Michigan. Once Promised, Now Stalled While the Cybertruck initially promised to revolutionize the pickup truck market, reality has proven more complicated. Parking lots are filling with unsold inventory in the U.S., while European countries have banned the vehicle entirely. And despite Tesla’s loyal fan base, many truck shoppers remain unconvinced. The Cybertruck remains a marvel of design and engineering — but increasingly, it’s also a case study in how innovation can collide with real-world safety, regulation, and consumer trust. In Farmington Hills, Michigan, Tesla stores over 100 unsold Cybertrucks in a disused shopping center.

articles.text: Piedmont resident Linda G. Arellano passed away peacefully at home on May 23rd surrounded by her loving family. Linda was kindhearted, outgoing, engaging and stylish, always with a flower on her lapel or pinned to her dress. She loved her family deeply and would light up any room the minute she walked in. An encounter with her always included her warm smile, a twinkle in her eyes, often a touch or hug, and the feeling of being loved. Born on December 26, 1939 and raised in Altadena, CA with two brothers, she was a true California girl. In 1957 she was named a Princess in the Pasadena Rose Parade. Linda attended UC Berkely and served as President of the Delta Gamma Sorority house after which she married her first husband of 12 years and settled in Piedmont. For the last 38 years, she shared a beautiful life with her treasured husband, Rick. While raising her three children as a single parent, she was engaged in interior design and worked as an Office Manager at Grey Advertising, as an Executive Director at Easter Seals of the East Bay, and as Senior VP of Communications at Grubb & Ellis, ringing the bell on Wall Street when they went public. In later years, she assisted Rick in his financial advisory business. She was also known for her culinary skills and catered events with her friend Nancy Martz. Linda and Rick were members of Claremont Country Club since 1987 where she served as Chair of the House Committee for several years. She enjoyed sailing as Rick’s first mate as well as tennis, golf, travel, and frequent games of dominoes. She was a knowledgeable and diehard football fan, cheering for the Cal Bears and the San Francisco 49ers. Linda Arellano died on May 23 at age 85. Linda was a woman of deep faith. She served as a Eucharistic Minister and a choir member at St. Theresa Catholic Church in Oakland. She also was a Dame of the Knights of the Holy Sepulcher. She is survived by her beloved husband, Rick (J. Richard) Arellano, and her three devoted children, Lisa Clawson (Steve), Geoff Greenlee (Sonia), and Phyllis Walker (John) and her two treasured granddaughters, Sydney Rae Greenlee and Justine Linda Greenlee. In addition, she leaves behind her five stepchildren Lorelei (Koby), Chris, David (Michelle), Pamela, Gregory (Terry), and their eight children. A funeral mass will be held at St. Theresa Catholic Church, 30 Mandalay Rd, Oakland, on Friday, June 20 at 11:00 a.m. with a reception immediately following. In lieu of flowers. the family suggests a donation to your favorite charity or the Susan G. Komen Foundation.

articles.text: Part 11 in a series In the history of Piedmont, two saloons have quenched the thirst of residents and visitors. One saloon was in a respected hotel. The other was fraught with problems. The Piedmont Springs Hotel was built to serve visitors to the Piedmont hills and the mineral springs in Piedmont’s Bushy Dell Creek. Built in 1871 as a first class resort, the hotel had 20 rooms and a main dining room with a crystal chandelier and velvet drapes. The Grand Saloon (for gentlemen only) had a long mahogany bar, billiard table, spittoons and a pot-bellied stove in the corner. The Grand Saloon gained brief notoriety in 1891 when the wives of some of Piedmont’s more prominent businessmen petitioned the county to rescind the hotel’s liquor license. The women objected to their husbands stopping for a drink on their way home. The license was never rescinded, and the Piedmont Springs Hotel continued to serve liquor for another year before it burned to the ground in 1892. A Mon Chateau Piedmont’s other saloon was A Mon Chateau. As far back as the 1870s, today’s Grand Avenue was known as Pleasant Valley Road. It ran through a very pleasant valley – sunny, free of wind, rolling hills, scattered trees – that extended from Lake Merritt into the Piedmont hills. It was the route that many early Oakland residents took from downtown Oakland to picnic in the Piedmont hills. Today, that road is Grand Avenue until it crosses the city line near Rose Avenue. It continues as Pleasant Valley Road in Oakland until it crosses Broadway and becomes 51st Street. In 1892, Axel R. Gruggel built a restaurant at the southwest corner of today’s Grand and Linda Avenues and served refreshments to these travelers into the Piedmont countryside. He called it “A Mon Chateau” (My Castle) and advertised it as a family resort and French restaurant. Taking advantage of the mild weather, he built a beer garden on the Linda Avenue side of the restaurant. During its first years, A Mon Chateau was a quiet, slow-paced retreat, but that changed with the 1906 earthquake. With the influx of San Francisco refugees to the East Bay, the surrounding land began to fill with new houses and residents. From 1903 on, A Mon Chateau had a series of owners with a series of troubles. Gruggel sold the restaurant to George Atcheson in 1903. He ran A Mon Chateau for a few years but encountered problems with his employees stealing liquor. In 1907, three bachelors began operating the restaurant. Thomas P. Fenton, George P. Mahoney and John F. Jennings lived on the second floor of the building and advertised it as “A pleasant place in Pleasant Valley [to eat dinner]. Dinner prepared by Emil Lotz, former chef of Poodle Dog, San Francisco.” Dinners were $1.00. Patrons were advised to take the Oakland Avenue streetcar, get off at Sunnyside Avenue and take a short walk to Pleasant Valley. The bachelor owners also advertised A Mon Chateau as a saloon and sold wine, liquor and cigars besides serving dinners. Soon, neighbors began objecting to what was becoming a boisterous saloon. When the new City of Piedmont (1907) passed its liquor licensing regulations, A Mon Chateau’s application for a liquor license was denied. Nonetheless, the three owners continued to sell liquor at A Mon Chateau without a liquor license. The following year in March 1908, all three were arrested and their liquor confiscated. Three months later in June of 1908, A Mon Chateau opened under new management and continued to advertise itself as a “First Class Restaurant and Family Resort.” New owners Seeger & Thomas continued to operate it as a restaurant, but without a liquor license the number of diners dwindled. In 1911, Rudolph Kohn took over the business. He sought a new way to attract more patrons. He called the former restaurant “The Piedmont Casino” and opened two rooms upstairs for those who enjoyed playing poker and faro. However, gambling was also illegal. The casino was raided in 1912, and nine card-playing patrons were arrested and fined $55 each. The casino closed shortly thereafter. Chateau had become the Grand Avenue Grocery Company, and business thrived. It may not have been a good location for a saloon, but it was an excellent spot for a grocery. Residents in the rapidly growing residential neighborhood could walk to the market at the corner of Grand and Linda Avenues. Proprietors changed, and the grocery business grew. By 1922, the grocery had become the Del Monte Market, run by Jack Ruedy and William VanLoo, who lived upstairs with their wives. The market sold meats, vegetables and delicatessen items. Ruedy and VanLoo added a new storefront, a drug store (Raymond’s Drugs), and built a bakery in the former beer garden to offer freshly baked breads to their customers. In 1930, George W. Leisz and his son Jacob H. Leisz were running the grocery store. The grocery store thrived until 1937 when new supermarkets began pushing out neighborhood grocery stores. It was the route that many early Oakland residents took from downtown Oakland to picnic in the Piedmont hills. Today, that road is Grand Avenue until it crosses the city line near Rose Avenue. It continues as Pleasant Valley Road in Oakland until it crosses Broadway and becomes 51st Street. In 1892, Axel R. Gruggel built a restaurant at the southwest corner of today’s Grand and Linda Avenues and served refreshments to these travelers into the Piedmont countryside. He called it “A Mon Chateau” (My Castle) and advertised it as a family resort and French restaurant. Taking advantage of the mild weather, he built a beer garden on the Linda Avenue side of the restaurant. During its first years, A Mon Chateau was a quiet, slow-paced retreat, but that changed with the 1906 earthquake. With the influx of San Francisco refugees to the East Bay, the surrounding land began to fill with new houses and residents. From 1903 on, A Mon Chateau had a series of owners with a series of troubles. Gruggel sold the restaurant to George Atcheson in 1903. He ran A Mon Chateau for a few years but encountered problems with his employees stealing liquor. In 1907, three bachelors began operating the restaurant. Thomas P. Fenton, George P. Mahoney and John F. Jennings lived on the second floor of the building and advertised it as “A pleasant place in Pleasant Valley [to eat dinner]. Dinner prepared by Emil Lotz, former chef of Poodle Dog, San Francisco.” Dinners were $1.00. Patrons were advised to take the Oakland Avenue streetcar, get off at Sunnyside Avenue and take a short walk to Pleasant Valley. The bachelor owners also advertised A Mon Chateau as a saloon and sold wine, liquor and cigars besides serving dinners. Soon, neighbors began objecting to what was becoming a boisterous saloon. When the new City of Piedmont (1907) passed its liquor licensing regulations, A Mon Chateau’s application for a liquor license was denied. Nonetheless, the three owners continued to sell liquor at A Mon Chateau without a liquor license. The following year in March 1908, all three were arrested and their liquor confiscated. Three months later in June of 1908, A Mon Chateau opened under new management and continued to advertise itself as a “First Class Restaurant and Family Resort.” New owners Seeger & Thomas continued to operate it as a restaurant, but without a liquor license the number of diners dwindled. In 1911, Rudolph Kohn took over the business. He sought a new way to attract more patrons. He called the former restaurant “The Piedmont Casino” and opened two rooms upstairs for those who enjoyed playing poker and faro. However, gambling was also illegal. The casino was raided in 1912, and nine card-playing patrons were arrested and fined $55 each. The casino closed shortly thereafter. By 1914, the former A Mon Chateau had become the Grand Avenue Grocery Company, and business thrived. It may not have been a good location for a saloon, but it was an excellent spot for a grocery. Residents in the rapidly growing residential neighborhood could walk to the market at the corner of Grand and Linda Avenues. Proprietors changed, and the grocery business grew. By 1922, the grocery had become the Del Monte Market, run by Jack Ruedy and William VanLoo, who lived upstairs with their wives. The market sold meats, vegetables and delicatessen items. Ruedy and VanLoo added a new storefront, a drug store (Raymond’s Drugs), and built a bakery in the former beer garden to offer freshly baked breads to their customers. In 1930, George W. Leisz and his son Jacob H. Leisz were running the grocery store. The grocery store thrived until 1937 when new supermarkets began pushing out neighborhood grocery stores. Piggly Wiggly opened a supermarket at the other end of the block at Sunnyside and Grand Fenton, Maloney and Jennings ran A Mon Chateau in 1907 and 1908. Note the arched opening to the beer garden on the far right. The building was the Grand Avenue Grocery Company in 1915. The grocery enclosed the porch and added large windows. The distinctive gabled roofs of A Mon Chateau are recognizable. (Photo, c. 1915) Avenue, and the Leisz grocery closed in 1935. The old A Mon Chateau building was torn down in 1936 when the Richfield Oil Company built a gas station on the corner lot. In the late 1960s, the business became the Phillips Gas station run by O.N. Gooch and Bernard’s Auto Repair. In the 1970s it became a Chevron Service Station operated by Leo Kraft. When Chevron sold the property in 1987, developer Patrick Ellwood had a two-story building constructed, and Leo Kraft Automotive Service continued in business on the Sunnyside side of the building. articles.text: Piedmont’s quiet and respectful community of birders have been gathering on the sidewalk of Moraga Avenue to see a bald eagle nest above the nearby cemetery, complete with two recently-hatched eaglets. The nest was first seen by neighborhood residents in late summer of last year. The nesting eagles frequented the area for the following months, appearing to settle into place around April of this year. On May 18, the birders observed two of America’s national birds feeding their young and captured long-distance photos of the eaglets and their parents. Knowledgeable birders at the scene estimate that the young birds were about two weeks old at the time. “I’m astounded every day I come out,” said one local resident. “I get goosebumps. My favorite is when they fly into or out of the nest – they’re just majestic birds. A bald eagle feeds one of its eaglets on May 18. Knowledgeable Piedmont birders estimated the chicks to be about two weeks old at the time. And then it’s been fun to watch the development of the eaglets.” Currently, one of the parents can sometimes be found in a tree adjacent to the nest, appearing to stand watch. According to nearby bird watchers, the most popular viewing spot is frequented by a retired Harvard professor who graciously answers questions about the nesting eagles. For residents interested in seeing the birds themselves, the Post asks its readers to be respectful of the birds habitat and safety, and to follow the lead of the more experienced birders for bird-watching etiquette. An adult bald eagle stands guard in a nearby tree. A young eagle stands atop its nest on June 9. Interested birders watch the nest carefully.
